headline: Highest risk is data leakage: Rasa can egress to allowlisted APIs while awesome-prompts is a prompt-content source with no isolation or provenance controls.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-prompts is a content-writing/prompt repository with no io_surfaces or sandboxing, while rasa is a customer-support bot that ingests dialogue and connects to messaging APIs. If content from agent_a is copied into agent_b workflows, prompt-like text can steer behavior. The pair lacks documented provenance or isolation, so the interaction is plausible in default use.
conditions: IF agent_a content is pasted into agent_b prompts or training data
IF agent_b treats imported text as instructions rather than data
mitigations: Use a fixed delimiter and instruction/data separation for imported text
Review copied prompt packs before loading them into agent_b
Disable any auto-ingest of repository text into live conversations
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to imported content

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a is docs-only and shows no data classes touched, but agent_b handles text and voice and can send traffic to allowlisted third-party APIs. If the pair shares a workspace or copied artifacts, agent_b can transmit content derived from agent_a beyond the local environment. The evidence is indirect, so medium is appropriate rather than high.
conditions: IF agent_a artifacts contain sensitive text and are imported into agent_b
IF agent_b forwards conversation context to an allowlisted external API
mitigations: Keep agent_a artifacts out of agent_b runtime inputs
Restrict agent_b integrations to a test tenant
Redact sensitive text before handoff
Audit allowlisted endpoints before enabling them
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a has no write, network, or concurrency surfaces documented, while agent_b supports multiple external API channels but explicitly does not support multiple instances. There is no evidence of overlapping mutable-resource writes, so direct capability conflict is limited. Uncertainty remains because agent_a's runnable surface is unverified, so low is the safer choice.
conditions: IF both agents are configured to write the same external resource
IF agent_a is deployed with undocumented write permissions
mitigations: Assign separate workspaces and credentials
Avoid concurrent edits to shared tickets or chats
Run only one writer per resource
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable state

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a produces prompt content that agent_b could reuse in customer-support dialogue. Because agent_b is a support bot with external messaging integrations, unverified prompt material can cascade into user-facing responses or actions. There is no documented verification step between them, but the pathway is indirect rather than clearly automated, so medium fits.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a output as authoritative response content
IF agent_b sends that content to customers through a connected channel
mitigations: Require human review before publishing generated replies
Compare outputs against a source-of-truth knowledge base
Limit agent_a content to draft-only use
requires-engineering: add verification gates before outbound messages

E_compliance.rationale: No residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented in either profile. agent_a is an open-source prompt repository with no touched data classes, while agent_b handles text and voice and may integrate with external messaging services. The compliance pathway is therefore speculative and limited to possible policy mismatch if sensitive support data is introduced.
conditions: IF regulated customer data is routed through agent_b
IF agent_a content is stored under a different retention policy than agent_b data
mitigations: Document data-class handling for both agents
Keep regulated data out of prompt repositories
Review retention settings on connected channels
requires-engineering: align residency and retention policies
